Without A, B would only match already-lowercase stored tags; without B, A's stored tags wouldn't be findable by mixed-case filters. Together, 'Dragons' stored as 'dragons' and filtered with 'Dragons' resolves to 'dragons', which matches. The only residual gap is pre-existing mixed-case tags in the DB, which neither change creates or worsens, and the redundancy of normalization on both sides is intentional and harmless.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change B adds a 60s in-memory cache to GET /api/tags and invalidates it only when articlesCreate creates tags. Change A makes article deletion also delete orphaned tags via prisma.tag.deleteMany, but never calls invalidateTagsCache. In the merged code, a client who calls GET /api/tags (populating the cache with ['solo','shared']), then deletes the article that was the only user of 'solo', will still get 'solo' from GET /api/tags for up to 60 seconds, even though the tag no longer exists in the database. B's cache correctness assumes tags only change through article creation, and A's change introduces a new tag-mutating path that breaks that assumption. A's test queries prisma directly, and B's tests do not delete articles, so neither catches this.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes userUpdatePrisma hash any password it receives. Change B's new userChangePassword controller already hashes the new password with hashPassword before calling userUpdatePrisma. In the merged code, the POST /api/user/password path therefore hashes twice: bcrypt(bcrypt(newPassword)) is stored. Login compares the plain password against the stored hash, so after a password change through the new endpoint the user can no longer log in with the new password (and the old password also fails), locking them out. B's own test only checks that the stored value differs from the plain text and from the previous hash, so it still passes. This is a runtime conflict that neither change causes alone: B was correct against the pre-A userUpdatePrisma, and A is correct for the PUT /api/user path.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: A makes Article.updatedAt auto-update via @updatedAt (and drops the manual updatedAt in articleUpdatePrisma). B adds a views counter that is incremented via prisma.article.update on every GET of an article. With @updatedAt, every update call, including B's views increment, now bumps updatedAt. So merged, merely reading an article changes its updatedAt, which is exposed in articleViewer and used as the sort key (orderBy updatedAt desc) in articlesListPrisma. Concrete scenario: a popular article viewed repeatedly floats to the top of the article list and shows a misleading 'updated' timestamp, even though no content changed. Also favorite/unfavorite updates would bump it too, but that is within A's own change. Neither change alone produces view-driven updatedAt churn. Additionally, the GET response is built from the article fetched before the increment, so it shows the stale updatedAt, creating inconsistent timestamps between reads.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem (unused tags of deleted articles should not appear in the tag list) in two different ways: A physically deletes orphaned tags on article delete, while B filters orphaned tags out at read time in getTags. Each makes the other redundant, and each ships a near-identical integration test for the same scenario. A also introduces a runtime hazard B does not: the global deleteMany of tags with no articles is not atomic with article creation (tagsCreatePrisma upserts tags before the article is connected), so a concurrent article create could have its freshly upserted tag deleted before it is attached. Overall this is duplicated/contradicting intent.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes fix the same bug (the feed returning articles from all authors). A filters in the database query with a `where` on followedBy, and B filters in the controller by post-filtering the results against currentUser.follows. Merged, the filtering is duplicated across two layers, so the intent overlaps. Behavior stays correct in practice because the two filters are logically equivalent, and the DB filter makes B's in-memory filter a no-op. The results don't differ. The tests also both pass after merge since identical assertions hold. The only real downside is redundant code and a mildly confusing design, not wrong behavior. Still, it is the same problem solved twice in different ways, which fits the 'intent' conflict definition, though no concrete runtime failure exists.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes add the same author-only check for article deletion: A inlines it in the articlesDelete controller, B adds a requireArticleAuthor middleware on the DELETE route. Merged, every delete request runs the same ownership check twice (user lookup plus article lookup in the middleware, then again in the controller). Behavior stays correct: non-authors get 403 from the middleware, authors pass both checks, and unknown users or slugs fall through to the controller's existing 401/422 paths. Both tests (deleteOwnership and deleteAuthorOnly) pass. Both also remove the same 'known bug' test, which merges cleanly. The conflict is intent: two redundant implementations of the same fix, with duplicated DB queries and duplicated authorization logic that can drift apart.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes address long titles at different layers, but they do not contradict each other. B rejects titles over 150 characters at the validator, so valid titles reach slugfy. A's slugfy truncates slugs to at most 100 characters and strips a trailing dash, which is safe for any input. Titles between 101 and 150 characters become 100-character slugs, an intended outcome. A possible runtime issue would be slug uniqueness, since longer titles that share a 100-character prefix would collide. But the original slugfy already had no uniqueness guarantee, and A's truncation does not interact with B's validation to create a new failure. The two changes' tests are independent and both hold in the merged code.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds database indexes on Article.authorUsername and Article.updatedAt. Change B adds a sort query parameter that orders by createdAt or updatedAt. The two are complementary: the updatedAt index supports the default ordering, and the createdAt ordering is simply unindexed. Indexes do not change query results, so the new tests and behavior remain correct. A migration may or may not exist, but that does not create a behavioral conflict. Neither change breaks an assumption the other relies on, and they do not duplicate work.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: A's cache is invalidated by a Prisma middleware on writes to the Tag or Article models. B's new orphan-tag cleanup issues prisma.tag.deleteMany, which is a write on the Tag model, so the middleware drops the cache. Article deletion is itself an Article write that clears the cache, and the follow-up tag cleanup clears it again after the deletes finish. Both are awaited before the response, so a subsequent GET /api/tags re-reads and sees the cleaned-up tag list. The one possible stale window is a getTags request that read tags before the deletes and sets the cache after invalidation, but that race exists in A alone and is not introduced by the merge. B's deleteMany action is covered by WRITE_ACTIONS. The two changes work correctly together.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes address plain-text password storage but on different paths. A hashes the password inside userUpdatePrisma (used by PUT /api/user); B adds a separate POST /api/user/password endpoint that hashes in the controller and writes through a new userSetPasswordPrisma, which bypasses userUpdatePrisma. Since B's flow never passes through userUpdatePrisma, there is no double hashing. B's endpoint gives no way to reach A's hashing, and A's hashing doesn't touch B's. Both produce correct hashed passwords, and login works for both. The overlap is a design redundancy (two ways to change a password), but not a contradiction or a runtime failure. A's removal of the old 'unhashed' test doesn't affect B's tests.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A renames the JWT_SECRET env var to AUTH_JWT_SECRET in the authenticator, createUserToken, tests, README and .env.test. Change B adds a separate RESET_TOKEN_SECRET env var and new password reset token code, and edits .env.test by adding a line at the end. The two .env.test edits touch different lines and merge cleanly: the result has AUTH_JWT_SECRET and RESET_TOKEN_SECRET. B's code and tests only use RESET_TOKEN_SECRET and never reference JWT_SECRET, and A's changes never touch RESET_TOKEN_SECRET. Nothing in B depends on the renamed variable, and the two changes solve unrelated problems, so I see no concrete scenario where the merged code breaks or duplicates work.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes set a page size for GET /api/articles in different places. A changes the default limit in articlesListPrisma from 20 to 10 (applies when no limit is passed), and its new test asserts the default list returns 10 articles. B adds ?page=N and hardcodes PAGE_SIZE = 20 in the controller, with a test asserting page 1 returns 20 articles. In the merged code, a plain request without page returns 10 articles, while ?page=1 returns 20. Page 2 starts at offset 20, but page-less pagination steps by 10. The two tests also contradict each other on how many articles come back from the same endpoint. Both changes define the page size of the article list with different values, so the merged endpoint is inconsistent with itself.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds a logger.info call after article creation in articlesCreate; Change B adds a MAX_TAGS validation that returns 422 before any tags or article are created. These edits touch different parts of the function and compose cleanly: oversize tag lists return early with no article and no log line, which is correct, since nothing was created. Valid requests still log and return 201. A's test uses a title with no tags, and B's tests only check status and tag counts, so neither breaks the other. No duplicated or contradictory intent.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A only refactors how the where clause is built in articlesListPrisma. Behavior is identical for defined values; for empty strings it now skips filters (previously empty-string author would filter to nothing, tag '' would filter by tagName ''), which is an edge case. Change B's new controller calls articlesListPrisma with a non-empty username from route params, undefined tag/favorited, and limit/offset undefined which fall back to defaults. The refactor does not break B's usage; they are compatible and don't duplicate work.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: The two changes add unrelated read-only count endpoints: one for comments on an article (/api/articles/:slug/comments/count) and one for articles per tag (/api/tags/:tag/count). They live in different routers and controller folders, with distinct URL paths. The only overlap is that both read db:article, which is shared read access with no mutation or changed assumptions. No route shadowing occurs, and neither solves the same problem as the other.

rows.label: no_conflict
rows.explanation: Change A only adds JSDoc comments and a docstring to userUpdatePrisma, with no behavior change. Change B adds trimming of bio and image inside the same function plus an integration test. The merged result keeps B's trimming logic and A's documentation. The JSDoc says 'Fields left out are kept', and B's code sets bio/image to undefined when absent, which Prisma ignores, so that remains accurate. No concrete scenario of incorrect behavior or duplicated work.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A converts article deletion into a soft delete (sets deletedAt) and filters deleted articles out of the article get/list/feed queries. Change B adds a /api/tags/counts endpoint whose getTagCounts counts articles per tag via prisma.tag._count.article, with no deletedAt filter. After merging, soft-deleted articles keep their tag relations, so a tag whose only article was deleted still reports count >= 1 and is returned, even though those articles are hidden everywhere else. Under the old hard delete, deleted articles dropped out of the count automatically, and B's `.filter(count > 0)` relied on that. A's soft delete breaks B's assumption, so the endpoint reports stale counts for tags attached to deleted articles; neither change shows this alone, and the existing tests (which never delete an article before checking counts) still pass.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Both changes solve the same problem (case/whitespace-insensitive emails) at different layers: A normalizes in the controllers, B normalizes inside the DB helpers. Merged, the email is normalized twice on both the register and login paths. Normalization is idempotent (trim + toLowerCase), so behavior is correct and there is no wrong runtime result, and both integration tests pass. It is redundant duplicated logic with two sources of truth, but no concrete failure scenario arises, so it is not a harmful conflict.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A makes article renames actually change the slug (the article's primary key / FK target). Change B adds a RecentView table that stores article slugs as plain strings with no foreign key or cascade. When an article is renamed after being viewed, RecentView rows keep the old slug. recentArticlesPrisma looks up articles by those stale slugs, finds nothing, and flatMap drops them silently, so the article disappears from every user's recent list even though it still exists under its new slug. Before A, the slug never changed on update, so B's slug-based reference was safe; A breaks that assumption. Additionally, if an article is deleted, orphaned RecentView rows also linger, but the rename case is the concrete cross-change failure. Stale rows also consume the take-10 window, so valid recent articles can be crowded out.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: After merging, articlesListPrisma orders by createdAt desc (Change A) but filters the cursor with updatedAt < before, where before is the cursor article's updatedAt (Change B). The sort key and the cursor key no longer match. Concrete scenario: articles One, Two, Three created in that order. If Three is edited later, its updatedAt is the newest while its createdAt is still newest. If instead Two is edited after Three was created, Two's updatedAt becomes greater than Three's. With ?limit=2 the list is [three, two]. Then ?after=two filters updatedAt < two.updatedAt, which returns One, but it also returns Three, since Three's updatedAt is below Two's edited updatedAt. That causes a duplicate across pages. Conversely, articles can be skipped when an article later in the createdAt order has a larger updatedAt than the cursor. B's pagination logic assumes updatedAt ordering, which A's change removes, so the cursor pagination is broken in the merged code. B's own test would fail in merged form if its pinned updatedAt order differs from createdAt order. In practice both sets are created sequentially, so createdAt order matches and the test passes, but real edits break it.

rows.label: conflict
rows.explanation: Change A adds an https-only rule for the image field, but only inside userUpdateValidator, which guards PUT /api/user. Change B adds a new route, PUT /api/user/image, which is not guarded by that validator. It accepts any string and writes it straight to the user's image via userUpdatePrisma. In the merged code a client can set image to "http://..." or "javascript:..." through the new endpoint, bypassing the rule A introduced for image updates. A's tests only exercise PUT /api/user, so they still pass. The two changes touch the same field with contradictory validation: the same invariant (images must be https) holds on one path and is violated on the other.
